a_rows_sample.anchor: We want to know whether there exists a corresponding state transformation T:K x I -> K such that F(That(H,i)) = T(F(H),i) for every valid H and input i. If this holds, then the history dynamics descend to the state space.
a_rows_sample.statement: Sets up the formal question of state sufficiency: given a history space H, a proposed state abstraction F:H->K, and a history-level transformation That:HxI->H, does a corresponding state-level transformation T:KxI->K exist such that F(That(H,i))=T(F(H),i) for all valid H,i -- i.e. do history dynamics descend to the state space.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H_A ~_F H_B iff F(H_A)=F(H_B). Then state sufficiency requires: H_A ~_F H_B => That(H_A,i) ~_F That(H_B,i). Thus ~_F must be a congruence with respect to valid transformations.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the equivalence relation ~_F induced by the state abstraction (H_A~_F H_B iff F(H_A)=F(H_B)) and states the central congruence requirement: this equivalence must be preserved by every valid transformation for the state representation to be sufficient.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Now suppose the proposed state representation retains only Content(K)={p}. ... Authorized(A)=true but Authorized(B)=false. Then F(That(H_A,validate)) != F(That(H_B,validate)). Yet initially F(H_A)=F(H_B). Content-only K fails the congruence test. This is a genuine falsification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Falsifies a content-only knowledge state via a worked example: two histories with different evidence sources (A authorized, B not) collapse to the same content-only state, but a governance-sensitive validation transformation produces divergent outcomes (Validated vs Unvalidated) depending on the discarded source information -- a genuine congruence failure, showing content-only K is insufficient once authority-sensitive transformations are valid operations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose we enrich the state with lambda(e)=source(e). Now F(H_A) != F(H_B) ... The previous counterexample disappears. But this does not yet prove sufficiency. We have only shown one missing distinction has been restored.
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows adding a source/provenance field lambda(e)=source(e) to the state resolves the specific counterexample found, but explicitly cautions this only restores one missing distinction and does not establish global sufficiency -- more collapsed-but-behaviorally-different histories must still be searched for.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose H_C and H_D have identical Content and Provenance. But H_C was produced under policy pi_1 while H_D was produced under pi_2 ... F(H_C)=F(H_D) under a representation that omits policy history. But T(H_C,i) != T(H_D,i). ... Is Policy part of state, provenance, or external context? ... It is de
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a further counterexample: two histories identical in content and provenance but produced under different policies collapse to the same state under a policy-omitting representation, yet future validation depending on the original governing policy produces different results -- concluding whether policy belongs to state, provenance, or external context cannot be decided by convenience but is determined by transformation sufficiency (independently arriving at a question the parallel verifier track, S1602/S1603, was also attacking).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Two histories have the same proposition but different validity intervals theta_A(p)=[t0,t1), theta_B(p)=[t1,t2). Suppose a transformation asks CurrentVersion(S,t1+epsilon)? Then the two states produce different results. ... Temporal validity is not merely decorative metadata if temporal queries are
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows via a temporal-query counterexample (CurrentVersion(S,t1+epsilon)?) that a state representation omitting temporal qualification fails congruence when temporal queries are valid operations -- confirming temporal validity is functionally load-bearing, not decorative metadata.

a_rows_sample.anchor: e1->p and e2->not p. Compare K_A={p,e1} with K_B={p,e1,e2,not p}. A transformation T_assess may produce Assessment(K_A)=Supported but Assessment(K_B)=Conflicted. ... A state representation containing only the latest proposition K={p} would lose information necessary for future assessment.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a contradictory-evidence counterexample showing evidence multiplicity is semantically relevant: two states differing only in whether conflicting evidence is retained produce different Assessment outcomes (Supported vs Conflicted) under T_assess, so a state keeping only the latest proposition would lose information needed for future assessment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose an information component x can affect the result of a valid future transformation T(K,i). Then x cannot be discarded from the state abstraction unless it is recoverable from other state information. Formally: x is semantically disposable => x=f(K) for some reconstruction function f, or no va
a_rows_sample.statement: States a general disposability criterion generalizing all the preceding counterexamples: an information component x may be discarded from the state abstraction only if it is reconstructible from the remaining state (x=f(K) for some f) or no valid operation can distinguish states differing only in x -- giving a formal test for classifying any candidate field as state, metadata, provenance, external context, or truly redundant.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K=F(H) is a transformation-sufficient representation if all permitted future semantics can be determined from K, rather than the complete H. But we should not call K a sufficient statistic without qualification. ... K must be sufficient for the permitted KnowledgeOS transformation semantics.
a_rows_sample.statement: Draws an explicit but qualified analogy to the statistical notion of a sufficient statistic: a state K=F(H) is transformation-sufficient if all permitted KnowledgeOS transformation semantics can be determined from K rather than the full history H -- but the file cautions the statistical term applies to a specific model/parameter and should not be borrowed unqualified, since the KnowledgeOS requirement is broader (sufficiency for a whole permitted transformation semantics, not one parameter).

a_rows_sample.anchor: H ~ mu_H. Then K=F(H) induces a push-forward distribution mu_K = F_* mu_H. ... mu_K is a regime-level object, not necessarily part of K.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects the state abstraction to measure theory without making it foundational: if H is a random history with distribution mu_H, then K=F(H) induces a push-forward distribution mu_K=F_*mu_H (mu_K(A)=mu_H(F^{-1}(A)) for measurable A); explicitly classifies mu_K as a regime-level object, consistent with the parallel Step 246 finding (S1601) that probability belongs to a regime projection, not to K itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: F is a compression map. The question becomes: Is this compression lossless with respect to the semantics we care about? That is exactly the congruence question. ... F o That = T o F. This is the formal expression of state sufficiency.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the commutative-diagram criterion F o That = T o F as the formal expression of state sufficiency (the state abstraction F is a compression map; sufficiency means the compression is lossless with respect to the transformation semantics), calling it one of the strongest formal tests obtained in the corpus so far, and gives the corresponding failure interpretation (a non-commuting diagram means the proposed state representation has lost necessary information).

a_rows_sample.anchor: K=(Content,Qualification,Governance) survives the experiments only if those components contain all information required by valid transformations. ... we should not yet assert K=(G,sigma,theta,lambda,pi) as a final decomposition. Instead: K must be defined by transformation sufficiency. This reverses
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the design question from 'what fields should a Knowledge State have?' to 'what information must a state preserve so that all valid KnowledgeOS transformations remain well-defined?'; explicitly withholds asserting K=(G,sigma,theta,lambda,pi) as final until it survives transformation-sufficiency testing -- a route to the same skepticism about the 5-tuple that the parallel verifier track reached by counterexample.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Minimality = systematic removal + congruence testing. This is far stronger than selecting the smallest-looking tuple. ... Minimality is always relative to the transformation language. ... Minimality(K) = Minimality(K | T). There may be no context-free 'minimal Knowledge State.'
a_rows_sample.statement: Reformulates minimality testing as systematic per-component removal followed by re-checking the congruence criterion (F^{-i} o That = T^{-i} o F^{-i}), rather than choosing the smallest-looking tuple by inspection; states the important architectural corollary that minimality is always relative to the transformation language T (Minimality(K)=Minimality(K|T)) -- there may be no context-free minimal Knowledge State, since a richer future transformation set can make previously-discardable information necessary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Transformation-Sufficiency Proposition: T:K x I -> K is semantically well-defined with respect to That iff F(H1)=F(H2) => F(That(H1,i))=F(That(H2,i)) for all valid H1,H2,i. Equivalently F o That = T o F. ... not yet a proven KnowledgeOS theorem, because the full transformation set has not been estab
a_rows_sample.statement: States the phase's central named proposition (Transformation-Sufficiency Proposition), giving a single precise, computationally testable mathematical criterion for when a state-level transformation is semantically well-defined relative to a history-level one -- explicitly labeled not yet a proven theorem because the full KnowledgeOS transformation set has not itself been established.

a_rows_sample.anchor: PASS -- Transformation congruence criterion established. FAIL -- Global state sufficiency not yet demonstrated. OPEN -- Minimal sufficient Knowledge State. ... K should not be defined independently of T. Instead, the pair (K,T) must be reconstructed together.
a_rows_sample.statement: Records the Step-248 verdict: PASS on establishing the congruence criterion; FAIL on demonstrating global state sufficiency; OPEN on minimal sufficient K; states the phase's major conceptual shift -- K must not be designed independently of the transformation set T, but the pair (K,T) must be reconstructed jointly -- and sets Step 249 as Transformation Algebra Reconstruction, to derive the corpus-supported transformation classes (T_create, T_observe, T_infer, T_validate, T_revise, T_reject, T_merge, T_supersede, ...) with domain/codomain/preconditions/postconditions/invariants/composability for each.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can two states with identical current representation produce different valid future behavior? ... If T(K_A)=K'_A and T(K_B)=K'_B with K'_A not equiv K'_B, then history affects future semantics. In that case, the compressed state K is not sufficient. This gives us a rigorous state sufficiency criteri
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the provenance-metadata-vs-constitutive question into a testable future-behavior criterion avoiding philosophical argument: if two states with identical current representation but different history produce different results under the same transformation, then the state representation is insufficient -- directly the criterion S1608 (Step 248) then executes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose they produce identical lineage edges. Yet the transformations had different policies pi_A != pi_B. If policy is semantically relevant, then lambda_A=lambda_B does not imply H_A = H_B. ... Potentially lambda=(source,transformation,actor,time,policy,evidence). But this is again a candidate str
a_rows_sample.statement: Falsifies plain parent-child lineage as a sufficient history compression: two histories can produce identical lineage edges while having been governed by different policies, so if policy is semantically relevant then lineage-equality does not imply history-equivalence -- proposing a richer candidate lambda=(source,transformation,actor,time,policy,evidence), still only a candidate structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: That requires: H_1 ~_H H_2 => T(H_1) ~_H T(H_2). This is a congruence condition. If it holds, the transformation descends from histories to states. ... State abstraction is valid only if it is transformation-compatible.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the congruence condition required for the equivalence-class definition of Knowledge State to be usable: ~_H must be preserved by every valid transformation (H1~_H H2 => T(H1)~_H T(H2)), so that transformations descend consistently from histories to their equivalence classes -- directly foreshadowing S1608's F o That = T o F criterion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What is the smallest mathematical structure that satisfies all non-negotiable requirements? Construct a sequence K0 -> K1 -> K2 -> ... where each added component must have a demonstrated necessity. ... The final result must distinguish MINIMALITY PROVEN from MINIMALITY PLAUSIBLE from MINIMALITY NOT
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes a 'minimal adequate K' procedure: build up a sequence K0->K1->K2->... adding only demonstrably-necessary components (tested against 7 questions per candidate: forcing requirement, external representability, derivability, removal breakage, reconstructability, circularity, unwanted coupling), and introduces a 3-level minimality-confidence taxonomy (PROVEN / PLAUSIBLE / NOT ESTABLISHED) explicitly rejecting fewer-fields as a minimality argument -- complementing S1608's congruence-based removal test with a positive constructive procedure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We cannot yet remove Merge, Supersede, Split, Withdraw because the corpus may require them for capabilities that have not yet been tested. Therefore the minimality status is: NOT YET TESTABLE rather than: minimal set found.
a_rows_sample.statement: Declares minimality of the state-changing operation family NOT YET TESTABLE (not merely unresolved), since Merge/Supersede/Split/Withdraw cannot yet be safely removed given untested capability requirements -- consistent with S1608's mandate that minimality testing requires actual removal-and-congruence checks, not inspection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Add, Remove, Revise, Merge, Split, Supersede, Validate, Reject, Transform. ... What invariants survive these operations?
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 232 (tail) asks whether knowledge states form an algebraic structure under nine operations (Add, Remove, Revise, Merge, Split, Supersede, Validate, Reject, Transform), posing Add(K,x)?, Merge(K1,K2)?, Revise(K,x,x')?, Transform(K_A,C_A,C_B)?, and the key question of what invariants survive these operations.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathbb K=\{(G,\sigma,\theta,\lambda,\pi)\mid \text{state satisfies the domain invariants}\}. ... (\mathbb K,\mathcal O)
b_rows_sample.statement: The knowledge-state SPACE mathbb K (all admissible states satisfying domain invariants) is distinguished from a particular STATE mathfrak K_t at time t; rather than assuming a classical algebraic structure (ring/field/vector space), the appropriate initial object is a state-transition algebra (mathbb K, mathcal O) where mathcal O is the set of admissible operations.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Transformation\neq Validation. Validation:\mathbb K\times X\rightarrow Assessment while Transformation:\mathbb K\times Parameters\rightarrow\mathbb K.
b_rows_sample.statement: State-changing vs state-classifying operations: Transformation != Validation -- Validation: mathbb K x X -> Assessment (may merely produce an assessment) while Transformation: mathbb K x Parameters -> mathbb K (changes the state); validation may subsequently trigger a transition, corresponding to the DDD chain Command->Decision->Event->State, rated a much better model than treating CRUD as the architecture.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Add_x(\mathfrak K) is a partial operation. ... Remove_x:\mathbb K\rightharpoonup\mathbb K. ... Remove(E) may require Reassess(A).
b_rows_sample.statement: Addition Add_x:mathbb K -> mathbb K is a PARTIAL operation, defined only if Invariant(K')=True; Removal Remove_x:mathbb K -|-> mathbb K is likewise partial since an accepted item may depend on the removed one (A-dependsOn->E), so Remove(E) may require Reassess(A).

b_rows_sample.anchor: x_t\xrightarrow{revisedTo}x_{t+1}. Revision=new state+historical relation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Revision must not be modeled as overwriting (x_t <- x_{t+1}, destroying history) but as x_t -revisedTo-> x_{t+1}, giving Revision = new state + historical relation, naturally supporting lineage.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \sigma(x_1)=Superseded and \sigma(x_2)=Accepted. Currentness\neq Truth.
b_rows_sample.statement: Supersession differs from revision: x1 is retained as historical knowledge marked Superseded (sigma(x1)=Superseded) while x2 is Accepted, again demonstrating Currentness != Truth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Merge\neq SetUnion. ... Merge(K_1,K_2,C,P) ... compatible, redundant, complementary, contradictory, superseding. ... TextMerge\neq SemanticMerge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Merge is a partial, semantic operation Merge:mathbb K x mathbb K -|-> mathbb K, not naive set union (Merge != SetUnion) since sources may contain contradictory claims; a proper Merge(K1,K2,C,P) classifies relationships as compatible/redundant/complementary/contradictory/superseding -- giving the DDD principle TextMerge != SemanticMerge (a repository-level/Git merge is not necessarily a domain merge).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Split(Merge(K_1,K_2))\neq(K_1,K_2). ... non-invertible knowledge transformation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Split:mathbb K -|-> mathbb K x mathbb K is not a true mathematical inverse of Merge -- Split(Merge(K1,K2)) != (K1,K2) in general because merge may introduce derived information, reconciliation decisions, normalization, or conflict resolution -- an example of non-invertible knowledge transformation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: (\mathcal T,\circ) has the structure of a transformation semigroup, assuming closure. ... (\mathcal T,\circ,I) is at least monoid-like. ... We should not claim it yet as a theorem.
b_rows_sample.statement: The set of admissible transformations mathcal T with composition forms a candidate transformation semigroup (mathcal T, o) assuming closure, with an identity transformation I_K(K)=K making (mathcal T,o,I) at least monoid-like -- explicitly not yet claimed as a proven theorem, but architecturally useful for representing pipelines K3=(T3 o T2 o T1)(K0).

b_rows_sample.anchor: T_2\circ T_1 may be mathematically composable but not governance-valid. MathematicalComposition from GovernedComposition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Governance breaks naive composition: T1 authorized in context C1 composed with T2 (requiring ungranted authority) may be mathematically composable but not governance-valid, requiring MathematicalComposition to be distinguished from GovernedComposition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal T_G\subseteq\mathcal T ... T\in\mathcal T_G only if Authority(T)\land Policy(T)\land RequiredEvidence(T). ... we should not automatically call \mathcal T_G a semigroup.
b_rows_sample.statement: Governed transformations mathcal T_G subseteq mathcal T require Authority(T) and Policy(T) and RequiredEvidence(T); mathcal T_G is NOT necessarily closed under composition (T1,T2 in T_G but T2 o T1 not in T_G if the combined transformation crosses a governance boundary) -- an important mathematical correction against assuming T_G is a semigroup.

b_rows_sample.anchor: G(T,K,C,A,P)\in\{0,1\}. K'=T(K) only if G(T,K,C,A,P)=1. ... Evidence is a condition of admissibility, not merely metadata.
b_rows_sample.statement: Governance is formalized as a boolean constraint system G(T,K,C,A,P) in {0,1}: a state transition K'=T(K) is valid only if G(T,K,C,A,P)=1, and separately E(T) |= ReqEvidence(T,P) must hold -- evidence is a condition of admissibility, not merely metadata. Together these give the core transition rule K_{t+1}=T_t(K_t) subject to G(...)=1 and E_t |= ReqEvidence(T_t,P_t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: M_C(\Delta_t)\Rightarrow Governed(T_t). ... U_t=\varnothing. A governed knowledge system may transform information, but material semantic changes may not occur silently.
b_rows_sample.statement: Material-change condition, rated potentially one of the most important invariants in the entire architecture: M_C(Delta_t)=1 (materiality of the diff between K_t and K_{t+1}) implies Governed(T_t); reformulated elegantly as U_t = empty set where U_t is the set of undeclared material changes -- a governed knowledge system may transform information, but material semantic changes may never occur silently.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t\subseteq K_{t+1} ... Clearly not. ... HistoricalKnowledge(K_t)\subseteq HistoricalKnowledge(K_{t+1}). ... HistoricalMonotonicity.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge is NOT monotonic (K_t subseteq K_{t+1} fails since knowledge can be corrected/withdrawn/superseded/invalidated), but a weaker HistoricalMonotonicity holds: HistoricalKnowledge(K_t) subseteq HistoricalKnowledge(K_{t+1}) -- the system should not erase the fact that a knowledge state existed, even though Current(K_t) need not be monotonic while History(K_<=t) should normally grow.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Do not assume KnowledgeOS is a lattice. It may become a partial order over particular classes of knowledge states, but this requires proof.
b_rows_sample.statement: Whether knowledge states form a lattice under an information ordering K1<=K2 (K2 contains at least as much accepted information) is explicitly left open and cautioned against assuming, since contradictions complicate a least-upper-bound K1 join K2; likewise no universal statistical information ordering should be assumed given multiple incompatible candidates (entropy, KL divergence, Fisher information, posterior concentration).

b_rows_sample.anchor: F_Y=F_X\circ T^{-1}. ... Y must remain linked to X. This is exactly what lineage is supposed to preserve.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distributional transformation is a rigorous statistical-layer example of knowledge transformation: for X~F and measurable T, Y=T(X) induces F_Y = F_X o T^-1; when KnowledgeOS derives an engineering indicator Y from observed metric X, Y must remain linked to X via provenance/uncertainty/assumptions -- exactly what lineage is meant to preserve.

b_rows_sample.anchor: q_1,q_2\xrightarrow{f}q. ... Validity(q)=g(Validity(q_1),Validity(q_2),f).
b_rows_sample.statement: Derived knowledge q=f(q1,q2) gives a knowledge derivation graph q1,q2-f->q; dependency preservation proposes Validity(q) = g(Validity(q1),Validity(q2),f) so that invalidating q1 makes q suspect -- a candidate for deterministic validity propagation, illustrated by Requirement->ArchitectureDecision->ImplementationConstraint where superseding the Requirement triggers Supersession->ImpactAnalysis on the ArchitectureDecision, not necessarily invalidation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Impact(q)=Descendants(q). ... Reassessment(Impact(q)). This may become one of the most important practical capabilities of KnowledgeOS.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge impact propagation: Impact(q) = Descendants(q) in the provenance/semantic graph, so a material change to q triggers Reassessment(Impact(q)) -- rated potentially one of the most important practical capabilities of KnowledgeOS, and making the transformation algebra explicitly dependency-aware: Input+Context+Evidence+Authority+Dependencies -> Output.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Law 1 -- Traceability ... Law 2 -- Governance ... Law 3 -- Evidence ... Law 4 -- Semantic accountability ... Law 5 -- Historical preservation ... Law 6 -- Epistemic separation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Six candidate algebraic laws, rated much closer to architectural invariants than the earlier broad principles: L1 Traceability (exists L(T) for every material transformation), L2 Governance (Material(T)=>Authorized(T)), L3 Evidence (RequiredEvidence(T)=>Evidence(T)), L4 Semantic accountability (MaterialSemanticChange(T)=>Declared(T)), L5 Historical preservation (historical state not silently destroyed), L6 Epistemic separation (Status(q) != Content(q)).

b_rows_sample.anchor: All changes require human approval is a policy. It is not necessarily a universal architectural invariant. ... Every consequential transformation requires an authority mechanism appropriate to its risk and policy.
b_rows_sample.statement: Crucial distinction between invariant and policy: 'all changes require human approval' is a policy, not a universal invariant; the more general, robust invariant is 'every consequential transformation requires an authority mechanism appropriate to its risk and policy' (human approval, delegated authority, deterministic policy, or automated rule).

a_notations: F o That = T o F

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 's1608-transformation-congruence-and-state-sufficiency' POSSIBLY relates to 'step232-knowledge-state-algebra' (batch B0039). Note: Step 248's commuting-diagram congruence criterion (F o That = T o F) for whether a proposed Knowledge-State abstraction F:H->K is sufficient for a given transformation set; falsifies content-only K by counterexample, connects to sufficient statistics and a push-forward measure mu_K=F_*mu_H, and reformulates minimality as transformation-relative removal-testing rather than tuple-size comparison. Independently converges with the parallel verifier track's (S1603) conclusion that K cannot be defined independently of its transformation set.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T1,T2 in T_G does not necessarily imply T2 o T1 in T_G. The audit correctly identifies this as a closure failure. Therefore we must distinguish T from T_G. ... 'transformation algebra' = working name, not established mathematical classification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the assumption of a closed 'transformation algebra': the corpus's own Step-232 audit shows the governed transformation set T_G is not closed under composition (T1,T2 in T_G does not imply T2 o T1 in T_G), so the unrestricted collection T must be distinguished from the actually-governed T_G, and 'transformation algebra' is downgraded to a working name rather than an established classification.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1} = T_t(K_t) subject to G(T_t,C_t,A_t,P_t)=1 and E_t |= Req(T_t,P_t). The audit identifies this as the best-formed transition rule in the corpus. ... the latter is not yet executable, because |= and Req remain undefined.
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopts the corpus's best-formed transition rule K_{t+1}=T_t(K_t) subject to governance admissibility G(T,C,A,P)=1 and an evidence-satisfaction requirement E|=Req(T,P), separating state transition, governance admissibility, and evidence admissibility as three distinct functions -- while noting the evidence-satisfaction relation |= and the requirement function Req remain formally undefined and the rule is therefore not yet executable.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T(K) is not equivalent to Allowed(T,K). Instead Allowed(T,K,C,A,P,E) must be evaluated first. Then, if allowed: T(K,theta)=K'. ... This is directly supported by the corpus's separation of transition from permission to transition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes the architectural separation between a transformation's effect T(K) and its permissibility Allowed(T,K,C,A,P,E), proposing a pipeline (K,T,C,A,P,E) -> Admissible? -> K'=T(K,theta), grounded in the corpus's own separation of transition from permission to transition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 10 operations classified: Transform (State transition, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Validate (Assessment, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Add (Partial state operation, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Revise (PARTIALLY VERIFIED); Merge/Supersede/Split/Remove/Reject/Replay (OPEN).
a_rows_sample.statement: Classifies 10 mandate-required operations against the Step-232 audit: Transform, Validate and Add are corpus-established (with distinct roles: state transition, assessment, and explicitly partial operation respectively); Revise is only partially verified; Merge, Supersede, Split, Remove, Reject and Replay are all OPEN -- explicitly matching the detailed Step-232 audit rather than the earlier assumption that every operation belongs to one algebra.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Add_x(K) a partial operation. ... Add: K x X -harpoonup-> K. ... Add(K,x) may be undefined when x violates an invariant. Thus Pre_Add(K,x) must hold before the operation is defined.
a_rows_sample.statement: Preserves Add as an explicitly partial operation (K x X -harpoonup-> K, undefined when x violates an invariant, requiring a precondition Pre_Add(K,x)), preferring this over the mathematically dishonest alternative of treating Add as total.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Revise involves new state + historical relation. ... revision appears to involve two outputs: (K',r) where r in HistoryRelation. ... because the corpus does not explicitly type the historical relation, we must keep this PROPOSED rather than promoted.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes that Revise may actually produce two outputs -- the revised state K' and a historical relation r in HistoryRelation -- since the historical fact K leadsto K' is not necessarily part of K' itself, but keeps this candidate signature (K x X x X' -harpoonup-> K x HistoryRelation) explicitly PROPOSED, not promoted, since the corpus never types HistoryRelation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Validate: K x X -> Assessment. Validation may subsequently trigger a state transition. Therefore Validate != Transform. This is CORPUS ESTABLISHES. ... Validation -> Assessment while Decision -> Transformation is a candidate architecture. The exact Decision signature remains unresolved.
a_rows_sample.statement: Confirms as corpus-established that Validate (K x X -> Assessment) is categorically different from Transform, and that validation is not necessarily mutating -- a later Decision function (unresolved signature) may map an Assessment to a specific transformation T_d, giving the candidate two-stage architecture Validation->Assessment, Decision->Transformation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The corpus explicitly rejects Merge(K1,K2)=K1 union K2 as a sufficient definition: Merge != SetUnion. ... A merge must presumably determine: conflicting assertions; identity; provenance; temporal validity; epistemic status; duplicate objects; resulting invariants. But these are requirements to inves
a_rows_sample.statement: Records the corpus's explicit rejection of a naive set-union definition of Merge, listing 7 open requirements a real merge operation must resolve (conflicting assertions, identity, provenance, temporal validity, epistemic status, duplicate objects, resulting invariants) while explicitly refusing to invent a signature for any of them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: To determine whether one state supersedes another, we need some notion of K1 = K2 or at least identity of the relevant knowledge object. Since knowledge-state equality remains undefined, the operation cannot yet be formally closed. Supersede = OPEN and the blocker is: Equality.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies undefined Knowledge-State equality as the specific and sole blocker preventing Supersede from being formally closed -- a precise, load-bearing dependency rather than a vague open item.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The key question is whether removing an object means: deleting it; marking it invalid; superseding it; retracting its epistemic status; removing it from a projection while preserving provenance. These are mathematically different operations. Remove = UNDEFINED at signature level. ... Reject listed b
a_rows_sample.statement: Records Remove as undefined even at the signature level, since 'removing' could mean 5 mathematically distinct operations (deletion, invalidity marking, supersession, epistemic-status retraction, or projection-removal preserving provenance); records Reject as effectively abandoned in the audited corpus (OPEN); and records Replay as equality-dependent, since whether replay must reproduce K_n exactly or merely observationally returns to the still-open equality question.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the 'operation set' contains several different kinds of arrows: State transformations (K -harpoonup-> K)... Assessments (K x X -> Assessment)... Historical reconstruction (History x K0 -> K)... Governance predicates (T x C x A x P -> {0,1}). This is a typed family of operations, not yet one algebra.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reconstructs the operation set as a typed family of 4 categorically distinct kinds of arrows (state transformations, assessments, historical reconstruction, governance predicates) rather than one homogeneous algebra of K x X -> K operations -- a substantially stronger and more disciplined result than forcing every operation into one signature shape.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T2 o T1 in T_G iff the composed transformation satisfies the governance constraints. But even that needs a formal definition of G. ... Governance closure = structurally described, computationally unresolved.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the correct (conditional, not universal) closure criterion for composed transformations under governance: T2 o T1 is in T_G if and only if the composed transformation itself satisfies the governance constraints -- but notes this criterion cannot yet be evaluated since G's algorithm, though well-typed (G(T,K,C,A,P) in {0,1}), is absent; governance closure is structurally described but computationally unresolved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We should now reject the simplistic architecture: T = one closed algebra of state transformations. ... KnowledgeOS transformation system containing: state transitions, assessments, governance predicates, historical reconstruction, possibly decisions/events, with typed connections between them. Wheth
a_rows_sample.statement: States the step's central architectural conclusion, rejecting the simplistic 'one closed algebra' hypothesis in favor of a typed KnowledgeOS transformation system (state transitions, assessments, governance predicates, historical reconstruction, possibly decisions/events, all typed-connected), while explicitly leaving open whether this deserves the mathematical name category, partial algebra, transition system, or something else, per the governing mandate's instruction not to prematurely choose a structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: State represents domain knowledge. Assessment represents an evaluation of knowledge. Decision potentially represents a governed choice. Transformation changes domain state. Governance determines whether the transformation is admissible. History preserves/reconstructs evolution. These should therefor
a_rows_sample.statement: Maps the mathematical typed-arrow separation directly onto a DDD boundary test: State, Assessment, Decision, Transformation, Governance and History are 6 distinct domain roles that should not automatically collapse into a single Aggregate, entity, or service, citing the corpus's own warning against conflating bounded contexts, aggregates, database tables and domain events.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The hypothesis that KnowledgeOS has one closed transformation algebra over K is now weakened. ... KnowledgeOS has a typed transformation/assessment/governance system. ... The correct mathematical structure remains UNRESOLVED until equality, domains, composition and closure are fully specified.
a_rows_sample.statement: Concludes Step 249 by weakening the one-closed-algebra hypothesis to a typed transformation/assessment/governance system, explicitly leaving the correct final mathematical structure UNRESOLVED pending full specification of equality, domains, composition and closure -- and sets Step 250 (Knowledge-State Equality and Identity Gate) as the next mandatory test, since undefined equality is identified as blocking Merge, Supersede and Replay specifically.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Validate: K x X -> Assessment. ... validation may subsequently trigger a state transition. Therefore Validate not-in T_K ... Instead Validate in A where A = {K x X -> Assessment}. This is one of the strongest findings in Step 250.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Validate as the strongest-evidenced operation, explicitly excluded from the state-transformation family T_K and placed instead in the assessment family A={K x X -> Assessment} -- reiterated as one of the step's strongest findings, consistent with S1613's identical conclusion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Revise = partial state transition with historical consequence is the strongest current characterization. ... signature refinement still OPEN [Revise: K x X x X' -harpoonup-> K x HistoryRelation, unpromoted since HistoryRelation is untyped].
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Revise's characterization from Step 249: corpus-established as a partial state-changing operation with a historical consequence, but its exact richer signature (producing a typed HistoryRelation alongside the new state) remains open since HistoryRelation itself is untyped.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The corpus defines Remove_x: K -harpoonup-> K. The operation is explicitly partial because removing one item may invalidate dependent knowledge. This means Remove in T_K is currently defensible. And Remove is partial. This is a stronger result than we had at Step 249.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reclassifies Remove as CORPUS-ESTABLISHES (a partial operation Remove_x:K-harpoonup->K, since removing one item may invalidate dependent knowledge) -- the file explicitly calls this 'a stronger result than we had at Step 249', where the same operation was instead rated UNDEFINED at signature level (S1613); the two adjacent same-day step files disagree on Remove's status without either citing the other's specific verdict.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Add_x: K -harpoonup-> K is the mathematically safer formulation. The corpus explicitly calls it a partial operation. ... Supersede: at minimum, supersession requires identifying what is being superseded. That immediately creates an equality/identity dependency ... Supersede = UNRESOLVED with blocker
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Add as a corpus-established partial operation (constrained by Invariant(K')=True), and reaffirms Supersede as UNRESOLVED, naming its blockers precisely as Equality, Identity, and TemporalSemantics -- consistent with and sharpening S1613's identification of equality as Supersede's blocker.

a_rows_sample.anchor: S = (K, T, A, Q, E, H, D, G) [Knowledge states, State transformations T:KxI-harpoonup->K, Assessments A:KxX->Assessment, Queries Q:KxI->Result, Events E, History H, Decisions D, Governance G:TxCxAxP->{0,1}]. This is not yet the final KnowledgeOS mathematical structure. It is the smallest currently d
a_rows_sample.statement: Assembles the strongest current typed-family structure S=(K,T,A,Q,E,H,D,G) with 8 named components (knowledge states, partial state transformations, assessments, queries, events, history, decisions, governance predicates) -- explicitly not the final structure, but the smallest currently defensible typed candidate family, extending S1613's 4-arrow-kind classification with Queries and Decisions made explicit.

b_rows_sample.anchor: docs/knowledge/ is the Engineering Knowledge Platform (EKP): a governed, linted, deterministic knowledge graph with unique ids, typed relations, cycle detection, and controlled vocabularies for authority and lifecycle. It runs. I executed it. ... 250 steps of formal theory were written beside a work
b_rows_sample.statement: Discovers via a 1467-file corpus scan that docs/knowledge/ (the Engineering Knowledge Platform, EKP) is a running, executed, governed and linted implementation of much of the theory, yet of 311 numbered-step files across 250 distinct step numbers, exactly one (step 153) mentions it, and only via one word ('knowledge-graph'); 21-23 non-step files do reference it -- an independently discovered second instance of the Q7 assertion-layer loss pattern (S1605), now confirmed by scanning implementation references rather than theory content.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 31 distinct definitional statements yield six mutually incompatible types [composed local contracts (071); f(Irreversibility,Impact,Criticality) (092); Strong BC Candidate (127); BackwardTraceability (170); DeterministicAssurance (230, self-referential); a boolean]. Step 230's self-definition direct
b_rows_sample.statement: Finds 'Assurance' irreparably overloaded across 31 definitional statements collapsing into 6 mutually incompatible types (composed local contracts, a function of irreversibility/impact/criticality, a 'Strong BC Candidate' label, BackwardTraceability, a self-referential DeterministicAssurance, and a plain boolean); Step 230's self-referential definition directly contradicts the corpus's own imported Williamson result that assurance cannot recursively certify itself; and by the corpus's own most-repeated epistemological claim (assurance is strong only where executable, weak where prose), the corpus's own assurance concept is weak -- named completion blocker CB-1, a hard blocker on formal closure.

b_rows_sample.anchor: (K, Merge, empty) is a commutative idempotent monoid -- a JOIN-SEMILATTICE. Executed. ... Contradict is symmetric, irreflexive, and NOT transitive -- a tolerance relation, never an equivalence. Any construction treating contradiction as an equivalence class is wrong. ... Remove has no total inverse

b_rows_sample.statement: TEST 3, described as decisive: strength is policy-relative (the same underlying evidence produces a different grade under a different sufficiency-bar policy), whereas (S,R) polarity is policy-invariant (the polarity of the evidence itself does not change when the policy bar changes). Since a component whose value changes with policy cannot belong inside a policy-independent Sigma (citing the corpus's own boxed rule that Policy is NOT-IN Identity(K), Step 271 s271.3), the graded strength scale must live outside Sigma, in the assessment layer.

b_rows_sample.anchor: flipping (portfolio, threshold) pairs found: {len(flips)} ... The scale is at most ORDINAL, and any average / threshold / percentage rule over it is MEANINGLESS in Roberts' sense (first-order MT-3, here re-established exhaustively rather than by a hand-picked case). MT-5 also stands: no empirical relational structure was ever given for the scale, so even its ORDINALITY is assumed rather than established. NOTE, honestly: not every rule flips
b_rows_sample.statement: TEST 4 exhaustively re-establishes the corpus's own earlier finding MT-3 (that an ordinal scale under an arbitrary order-preserving re-encoding can flip the verdict of a mean/threshold decision rule) not via a single hand-picked example but via exhaustive search over three order-preserving encodings, all portfolio sizes 1-3, and all integer thresholds 1-7, finding multiple flipping (portfolio, threshold) pairs. Also reaffirms first-order finding MT-5: the strength scale's ordinality itself is assumed, never established via an empirical relational structure. Explicitly notes not every decision rule flips (min/max/median are invariant), so meaningfulness must be checked per-rule, not declared uniformly wrong.

b_rows_sample.anchor: THEREFORE: Sigma = P({Support, Refute}) policy-INVARIANT, derived from evidence ; Strength = f(evidence, policy) policy-RELATIVE, an ASSESSMENT output ... They are neither competing definitions of Sigma nor orthogonal dimensions. Step 275 and Step 272B answer DIFFERENT questions, and the contradiction dissolves once Assessment is separated from Sigma
b_rows_sample.statement: Final resolution of the Step 275 vs Step 272B tension: adjudicating five hypotheses about the graded strength scale S's relationship to Sigma -- (a) part of Sigma: NO, policy-relative while Sigma is not; (b) orthogonal: NO, refuted by nesting (Test 1); (c) derivable: YES, strength=f(evidence,policy) over the same evidence set Sigma derives from; (d) policy-dependent: YES, and this is precisely why it is excluded from Sigma; (e) obsolete: NO, three operations (Qualify, Assess, Compare) need it. Concludes Sigma is the coarsest policy-invariant abstraction of the evidence set, while Strength is a policy-relative refinement of that same evidence set produced by the Assessment layer -- Step 275 and Step 272B are answering different questions, not contradicting each other, once Assessment is properly separated from Sigma (per s271.10-11's Assessment != Truth, Assessment != Inference, and 272A.7).

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #1 — Knowledge as a generic object: forbidden in 208, used as an Owner in 210
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 208 Section 208.28 boxes a prohibition: the Data->Information->Evidence->Assessment->KnowledgeClaim transformations of semantic status 'should not [be collapsed] into one generic object called Knowledge.' Step 210 Section 210.25's matrix row I11 nonetheless assigns Owner='Knowledge' (and row I3 compounds it with 'Knowledge infrastructure'), the exact generic object Step 208 boxed a prohibition against two files earlier in the same band. Severity HIGH; neither Step-206 bounded context, and neither file notices.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #2 — Provenance composition (208) excludes the authority Step 209 requires
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 208 Section 208.25 asserts as an equality P(G)=P(A)∪P(E), boxed as 'provenance must be closed under semantic transformation.' Step 209 Section 209.4 requires Final(D)⇒DecisionBasis(D)∧Authority(D). Since Authority(D), the governance grant that made a decision final, is in neither P(A) nor P(E), a governed decision's provenance under Section 208.25 cannot contain its own authority, yet Step 209's own traceability requirement (Basis(D) including authority) demands that it does -- the two cannot both hold. Independently checked, the equality is additionally vacuous if closure holds (P(A)⊇P(E) implies the union is just P(A)) and self-refuting if it does not. Severity HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #3 — The evidence-strength scale is recalibrated between Step 210 and Step 212
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 210 Section 210.30 defines E_1=documentation, E_2=manual inspection, E_3=automated test, E_4=property-based test, E_5=formal verification. Step 212 Section 212.6 defines E_0=No evidence, E_1=Claim/documentation, E_2=Static implementation evidence, E_3=Executable test evidence, E_4=Runtime/production evidence, E_5=Formal verification. E_2, E_3 and E_4 disagree between the two files (only E_5 agrees), so a claim 'has E_4 evidence' means a property-based test under Step 210 and production observation under Step 212 -- entirely different assurance. Aggravating factor: Step 212's calibration silently matches the uncited Step 109's (E2=implementation, E4=runtime), so Step 212 restores an earlier convention without knowing it. Severity HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #4 — E_1 bound twice inside Step 210 itself
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 210 Section 210.20 writes E_1⇒P and E_2⇒¬P (evidence items entailing propositions); Step 210 Section 210.30, ten sections later, writes E_1=documentation (an ordinal assurance rung). Same symbol, same document, incompatible types, undisambiguated. Severity MEDIUM-HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #5 — Evidence/Test ordering reversed between Step 210's own boxed conclusion and Step 211's boxed conclusion
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 210 Section 210.40 boxes Invariant->Owner->Enforcement->Evidence->Test->Assurance; Step 211 Section 211.2 boxes I->Owner->Mechanism->Test->Evidence -- directly conflicting orderings, both boxed as conclusions in consecutive files. Step 210's own Section 210.1 tuple and Step 209's tail agenda both side with Step 211's ordering, so Step 210's boxed conclusion contradicts Step 210's own boxed tuple. Severity MEDIUM; the direction matters since Evidence->Test means evidence licenses the test while Test->Evidence means the test produces the evidence, which is what Steps 212-214 assume throughout.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #6 — min over assurance vs. the prohibition on scalarization, both boxed in Step 211
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 211 Section 211.6 states Assurance(I_global)<=min{Assurance(I_1),Assurance(I_2),...}; Step 211 Section 211.17 boxes 'Vector assurance is preferable to premature scalarization.' min over a set requires a total order on the codomain, but Section 211.9 makes assurance a 6-vector (only partially ordered), so evaluating min requires exactly the scalarization Section 211.17 forbids -- the two boxed positions of one file are mutually exclusive. Aggravated by Section 211.4's ordinal-only assurance-adjacent quantities and by Section 211.17's own use of cardinal values A_s=1, A_p=0, 0.83. Severity HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #7 — Step 212 builds ownership diagnostics and deletes the ownership data needed to run them
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 212 Section 212.15 boxes 'Ownerless Invariants' as a finding to explicitly search for (I exists but Owner(I)=empty set), yet Step 212 Section 212.4's register reprints all fifteen invariants with the Owner column removed (columns reduced to ID|Property|Target), and no search for ownerless invariants is performed anywhere in the file. Step 210's deleted Owner column contained exactly the data Sections 212.15/212.16 are designed to interrogate: 7 of 15 rows owned by a layer or pattern (effectively ownerless), 5 of 15 slash-shared. Severity HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #8 — F/D/P/U mandated in Step 213, applied zero times across Steps 213-215
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 213 Section 213.26 mandates that every important statement during reconstruction carry an [F]/[D]/[P]/[U] label ('our editorial control system'). A machine count of applied labels in Steps 213, 214, and 215 finds 4, 0, 0 respectively, and all four occurrences in 213 are the legend itself. Zero of the hundreds of statements in the three files that mandate the labels carry one, even though Section 213.26 explicitly scopes the requirement to these reconstruction documents themselves. Severity HIGH; this is a performative contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #9 — Step 214's self-assessment table violates Step 214's own boxed evidentiary rule eight lines later
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 214 Section 214.32 boxes 'no architectural claim should be stronger than the evidence supporting it.' Step 214 Section 214.33's final row states 'Risk of overclaiming | Explicitly controlled' -- a claim about the corpus's own overclaiming risk with zero supporting evidence, in a table that also self-awards 'Very strong' on five dimensions in a file containing no evidence at all. Severity MEDIUM-HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #10 — Three incompatible ledger arities inside Step 214
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 214 Section 214.1 boxes a 10-tuple EL_i=(Step,Artifact,Observation,Fact,Derivation,Decision,Architecture,Invariant,Evidence,Status); Section 214.6 gives a 15-field schema table; the Section 214 tail (line 1095) gives an 8-column matrix header whose columns barely overlap the 10-tuple's. Three incompatible schemas for 'the Evidence Ledger' in one file, with no reconciliation and no statement of which is normative. Severity MEDIUM.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #11 — Step 215 prohibits new formulas and mints three (four) in the same file
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 215 Section 215.30 prohibits 'creat[ing] more theoretical formulas merely because we can,' yet the same file mints R(S_i)=(O_i,L_i,A_i,V_i,U_i) (215.1), Convergence(I)=NumberOfIndependentEvidencePaths(I) (215.7), the boxed SemanticIntegrity∝DistinctionPreservation (215.10), and the boxed B=Synthesize(Evidence,Experiments,Failures,Insights,Architecture,PhilosophicalReflection) (215.32) -- four new formal objects, none computed. Severity MEDIUM; aggravated because the proportionality is not merely new but ill-typed, and Synthesize is never specified.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #12 — Step 215 exempts itself and its seven predecessors from its own discipline
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 215 Section 215.31 (Phase 1) targets S_1...S_182 -> EvidenceLedger, goal 'understand what actually happened'; the same file's closing paragraph defers 'what we previously called Step 183 onward' to a later decision about renaming or absorption. Steps 183-215 include all eight in-scope files of this verification, so the reconstruction discipline is scoped to exclude the very documents that mandate it -- compounded by Contradiction #8 (zero labels applied). Severity HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #13 — The scope of the derivation phase disagrees between Step 212 and Step 215
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 212 Section 212.5 states 'Steps 1-211 have largely been derivation'; Step 215 Section 215.31 and five other occurrences scope the reconstruction to S_1...S_182. The corpus states the derivation ran to 211 while scoping reconstruction to 182; the 29-step remainder is never reconciled, and 182 is never justified anywhere. Severity MEDIUM.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #14 — Subtraction on an undefined information measure, forbidden in Step 208 and performed anyway in Step 212
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 208 Section 208.10 writes L(C)=I_required-I_preserved and immediately cautions 'we should not treat this as a literal numeric quantity until we define an information measure.' Step 212 Section 212.19 writes L(C)=InformationBefore(C)-InformationAfter(C) without that caveat and without citing 208.10 -- no information measure is defined anywhere in the intervening four files. This is the fourth occurrence of the pattern in the band (208.3's I(A)<I(E), 208.10, 212.19, and 214.7's SemanticLoss(A)>0). Severity MEDIUM-HIGH.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #15 — Total order on epistemic strength declined in Step 209 Section 209.21 and then used in 209.25 and 210.9
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 209 Section 209.21 states Unknown≺Hypothesized≺Supported and explicitly declines a universal total ordering ('the actual epistemic lattice must be derived from the domain'). Step 209 Section 209.25 (S(T(x))>S(x)) and Step 210 Section 210.9 (Strength(T(x))>Strength(x)) both then use strict > on the same kind of quantity, presupposing the order that was just declined four sections earlier and never derived. Severity MEDIUM.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CONTRADICTION #16 — Invariants modeled as a dependency graph and as a flat conjunction, consecutively, within Step 209
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 209 Section 209.31 states that some invariants depend on others (HistoricalTraceability depends on Identity+Versioning+Provenance), illustrated with a 24-line ASCII dependency graph. Step 209 Section 209.32 then composes all invariants as a flat, order-free conjunction I_global=AND_{i=1}^n I_i. A conjunction cannot express dependency; the two sections model the same invariant set with incompatible structures, consecutively. Severity MEDIUM.

a_rows_sample.statement: Summary tally of Part 6's contradiction catalogue across Steps 208-215: 16 contradictions total, of which six are internal to a single file (#4, #6, #9, #10, #11, #16) and ten are cross-file within the band (#1, #2, #3, #5, #7, #8, #12, #13, #14, #15).
